The model's weights haven't changed.

But the KV memory requirement has increased eightfold.

This is why concurrency and context length are major determinants of inference memory.

Interactive: Full inference memory calculator

This combines both weight storage and KV-cache memory.

It uses two representative hypothetical dense decoder configurations, not a promise about any particular checkpoint.

Try three experiments:

  1. Keep the 8B model at 4-bit and raise concurrency from 1 to 8.

  2. Keep the weights at 4-bit but double the context length.

  3. Switch from BF16 KV cache to FP8 KV cache.

You'll see that weight precision and cache precision are independent controls.

Quantizing the model weights does not automatically quantize the KV cache.

Another worked example: A 70B-class model

Assume:

  • 80 layers.

  • Eight KV heads.

  • Head dimension 128.

  • BF16 KV cache.

  • Context length 8,192.

The KV memory per sequence becomes:

MKV=2(8192)(80)(8)(128)(2)M_{\mathrm{KV}} =2(8192)(80)(8)(128)(2)
MKV=2.5 GiB per sequence\boxed{M_{\mathrm{KV}}=2.5\text{ GiB per sequence}}

Four such sequences require:

10 GiB of KV cache\boxed{10\text{ GiB of KV cache}}

Now add 4-bit weights:

70×109×48=35 GB70\times10^9\times\frac48=35\text{ GB}

That's approximately 32.6 GiB of ideal weight storage.

So before overhead:

32.6+10=42.6 GiB32.6+10=\boxed{42.6\text{ GiB}}

This is already close to the usable capacity of a GPU advertised as having 48 GB.

Actual fit would depend heavily on the quantization scheme and runtime overhead.

And a 24 GB GPU wouldn't be sufficient for all those weights even with no KV cache, unless some of the model is offloaded or distributed.

5. Quantization — How can 16-bit weights become 4-bit weights?

We've calculated memory assuming 4-bit weights.

But what does that actually mean?

Remember a learned weight matrix from Deep Learning Basics:

W∈Rm×nW\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}

Each entry might be an ordinary floating-point value:

[−0.73, 0.18, 1.42, −0.09,…][-0.73,\ 0.18,\ 1.42,\ -0.09,\ldots]

If each entry is stored in BF16, it occupies 16 bits.

For billions of parameters, that's expensive.

Quantization maps a larger range of possible floating-point values into a smaller set of representable values.

The simplest idea: Scale and round

For a symmetric uniform quantizer, a simplified operation is:

q=clip⁡(round⁡(ws),qmin⁡,qmax⁡)q=\operatorname{clip}\left( \operatorname{round}\left(\frac{w}{s}\right),q_{\min},q_{\max} \right)

Where ss is a scale factor.

To approximately reconstruct the weight:

w^=sq\boxed{\hat w=sq}

The reconstructed value w^\hat w is generally not exactly the original ww.

That's quantization error.

A simple 4-bit quantization example

Original weight

Quantized integer

Reconstructed

-0.73

-4

-0.80

0.18

1

0.20

1.42

7

1.40

-0.09

0

0.00

Illustrative symmetric quantization using scale s = 0.2 and a signed 4-bit integer range of −8 through 7.

For instance:

w=1.42,s=0.2w=1.42,\quad s=0.2
q=round⁡(1.42/0.2)=7q=\operatorname{round}(1.42/0.2)=7
w^=7(0.2)=1.4\hat w=7(0.2)=1.4

The approximation error is:

∣1.42−1.4∣=0.02|1.42-1.4|=0.02

One small error may not matter much.

But a modern LLM contains billions of weights, and some tensors are more sensitive to quantization error than others.

That's why practical quantization techniques are more sophisticated than scaling the entire model with one global scale.

Group-wise quantization

Instead of one scale for a whole model, we divide weights into small groups.

Each group has its own scale, and sometimes a zero-point or other metadata.

For example, if a group contains 128 weights:

  • Each weight uses 4 bits.

  • The group uses one additional 16-bit scale.

Storage for the quantized values:

128×4=512 bits128\times4=512\text{ bits}

Scale overhead:

16 bits16\text{ bits}

Effective storage:

512+16128=4.125 bits per weight\frac{512+16}{128} =\boxed{4.125\text{ bits per weight}}

That's larger than exactly 4 bits per weight.

And we're still ignoring any other metadata or separately stored tensors.

This is why a real "4-bit" checkpoint isn't necessarily exactly one-quarter of its FP32 size.

The distinction interviewers care about

Quantized storage precision is not necessarily computation precision.

A model can store weights in 4-bit form but dequantize them inside a matrix-multiplication kernel and use BF16 or FP16 arithmetic.

So:

"The model is 4-bit"

does not automatically mean:

"Every operation runs using 4-bit arithmetic."

Hugging Face's bitsandbytes documentation explicitly distinguishes 4-bit weight quantization from the compute dtype. [2]

6. BF16, INT8, NF4, GPTQ, AWQ and GGUF — What do these terms mean?

These terms are often mixed together, even though they describe different aspects of quantization.

The most useful distinction is between:

  • Numerical formats: How values are represented.

  • Quantization methods: How values are converted and errors are controlled.

  • Checkpoint formats and runtimes: How models are stored and executed.

Numerical precision

Representation

Broad idea

Storage per value

FP32

Standard 32-bit floating point

4 bytes

FP16

16-bit floating point

2 bytes

BF16

16-bit floating point with a wider exponent range than FP16

2 bytes

FP8

8-bit floating point, with multiple possible formats

1 byte

INT8

8-bit integer, typically with scales

1 byte before metadata

INT4

4-bit integer, typically with scales

0.5 bytes before metadata

NF4

Nonuniform 4-bit codebook representation

0.5 bytes before metadata

BF16 is not quantization in the same sense as group-wise INT4 compression; it is a floating-point numerical format.

NF4 also deserves special attention because it appears in QLoRA.

The important quantization families

bitsandbytes 4-bit / NF4

An accessible approach to loading quantized Linear layers, widely associated with QLoRA. NF4 uses a nonuniform 4-bit representation designed for approximately normally distributed weights. We'll study its training use in Lecture 5.

GPTQ

A post-training quantization method that uses calibration information and approximate second-order error compensation to reduce reconstruction error when quantizing weights.

AWQ — Activation-Aware Weight Quantization

Uses activation information from calibration data to identify and better protect important weight channels during quantization.

GGUF

A model-file format used extensively with llama.cpp-compatible runtimes. GGUF files can store tensors using various quantization types, alongside model metadata and tokenizer information.

Hugging Face's quantization guidance distinguishes calibrated approaches such as GPTQ and AWQ from quantization methods that operate without calibration. [3][4][2]

Is GGUF the same as Q4?

No.

GGUF is a file/container format.

A GGUF checkpoint may contain different tensor quantization schemes.

For example, names such as Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M and Q8_0 refer to particular schemes or mixtures used in the llama.cpp ecosystem.

The effective bits per weight need not equal the integer in the name.

The llama.cpp quantizer's own reference examples list a Llama-3-8B Q4_K_M file around 4.58 GB—not exactly the 4 GB theoretical minimum for eight billion ideal 4-bit weights. [5]

Which should you use?

For local inference on a laptop or consumer computer, the available runtime and hardware backend often determine which format is convenient.

For a supported GPU serving stack, quantized checkpoints and kernels optimized for that accelerator may be preferable.

For adapter training with QLoRA, NF4 is especially relevant.

But the name of the format alone does not tell us the final model quality or inference speed.

We need to consider the model, quantization calibration, hardware, kernels, context length and workload.

Does quantization always make inference faster?

No.

It reduces weight storage, which can reduce the amount of data transferred from memory.

But converting the quantized values into a form usable by computation also costs work.

Some quantized kernels exploit hardware efficiently; others may suffer from conversion overhead or inadequate optimization.

Quantization can sometimes significantly reduce memory without improving throughput.

That's why memory efficiency and computation efficiency should be evaluated separately.

7. How fast could a quantized model theoretically generate?

Let's use a simple hardware reasoning exercise.

Suppose:

  • An 8B model uses ideal 4-bit weights.

  • Its weight storage is 4 GB.

  • A hypothetical GPU has memory bandwidth of 1 TB/s.

  • We serve one sequence at a time.

  • Each decode step effectively needs to stream the model weights from GPU memory.

Then a simplified lower bound for the weight-reading time is:

tweight read≳4 GB1000 GB/s=0.004 secondst_{\text{weight read}}\gtrsim \frac{4\text{ GB}}{1000\text{ GB/s}} =0.004\text{ seconds}

That's 4 milliseconds.

The corresponding weight-bandwidth ceiling is:

250 tokens/second\boxed{250\text{ tokens/second}}

But this is not a prediction of actual model speed.

It ignores the KV cache, compute, dequantization, memory access inefficiencies, launches, sampling and service overhead.

Also, GPUs with different memory bandwidths and optimized kernels produce different results.

What happens with BF16 weights?

Our 8B model would use approximately 16 GB of BF16 weights.

With the same simplified 1 TB/s bandwidth assumption:

t≳161000=0.016 secondst\gtrsim\frac{16}{1000} =0.016\text{ seconds}

That gives a weight-bandwidth ceiling of:

62.5 tokens/second\boxed{62.5\text{ tokens/second}}

Again, only under this simplified bandwidth model.

The 4-bit version potentially needs less weight-data movement.

But it may require additional processing and may not achieve the theoretical advantage.

Why does batching change this calculation?

Suppose we decode one token for eight different requests in a batch.

We can reuse the same model weights across the batch's matrix calculations.

We don't necessarily need to load the entire set of weights independently eight times.

This can improve arithmetic utilization and effective throughput.

However, each user has their own context and KV cache.

So batching creates a trade-off:

More parallel work can improve GPU utilization, but also increases KV memory requirements and scheduling complexity.

That is exactly where we'll begin Lecture 4.

8. Quantizing the KV cache itself

So far, we've mostly discussed weight quantization.

But we can also store keys and values at lower precision.

Suppose our 8B example uses:

  • 32 layers.

  • Eight KV heads.

  • Head dimension 128.

  • 8,192 cached tokens.

  • One sequence.

At BF16:

MKV=1 GiBM_{\mathrm{KV}}=1\text{ GiB}

If we store each key/value element using 1-byte FP8 instead of 2-byte BF16:

MKV,FP8≈0.5 GiB\boxed{M_{\mathrm{KV,FP8}}\approx0.5\text{ GiB}}

That's an approximately 50% reduction in the principal KV tensor storage.

Modern inference implementations support FP8 KV caching, although quantization scales, accuracy and kernel details matter. vLLM's 2026 technical analysis discusses both long-context numerical accuracy and practical latency/throughput trade-offs. [6]

Is FP8 KV caching always safe?

Not necessarily.

Quantizing K and V introduces numerical error into attention.

Those errors can affect attention scores and output representations, especially in sensitive layers or long contexts.

The effect depends on the model, scale calibration, numerical format and attention implementation.

Therefore, we'd normally evaluate:

  • Memory savings.

  • Output quality and task accuracy.

  • Long-context performance.

  • Actual decode latency.

  • Runtime compatibility.

The central lesson is simple:

Reducing KV-cache precision saves memory, but the quality and speed trade-offs must be measured.

9. What about model architecture: GQA, sliding windows and MoE?

Now we can connect the memory formula back to Lecture 1.

GQA

Reducing KV heads from 32 to 8 reduces the KV tensor storage by:

832=14\frac8{32}=\boxed{\frac14}

That's a 75% reduction at the same context length, layer count, head dimension and precision.

Sliding-window attention

A sliding-window layer may retain only the most recent WW positions needed by that layer's attention mechanism.

Its cache need not grow indefinitely with the entire context.

If all other assumptions remain unchanged, the corresponding layer's cache storage scales with roughly:

min⁡(T,W)\min(T,W)

rather than TT.

But hybrid models may include both sliding-window layers and full-attention layers, so we must account for them separately.

MoE

Mixture of Experts changes how many FFN parameters are activated per token.

It does not automatically multiply the attention KV-cache size by the total number of experts.

The KV cache comes from attention layers, while experts typically occupy the feed-forward portions.

Therefore, MoE total parameter size and KV-cache size are not determined by the same quantity.

That's an important distinction when sizing large MoE models.

10. Implement KV caching in PyTorch

Now let's build the most important mechanism ourselves.

We'll reuse the modern Transformer ideas from Lecture 1, but modify attention to accept and return a cache.

There are three things our implementation must get right:

First: Cache keys and values separately for each layer.

Second: Append only newly computed K/V tensors, rather than recomputing the previous ones.

Third: Apply RoPE using the token's absolute position within the sequence, not its position inside the current one-token input.

That third detail is surprisingly easy to get wrong.

Part A — RoPE with a positional offset

Previously, our RoPE implementation assumed positions started at zero.

During cached generation, a newly supplied token might actually be at position 1,000.

Its rotation must reflect position 1,000, even though the current input tensor contains only one token.

Python

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

def rope_with_offset(x, start_pos=0, base=10000.0):
    """
    x: (B, H, T, head_dim)
    start_pos: absolute position of first current token
    """
    B, H, T, D = x.shape
    assert D % 2 == 0

    positions = torch.arange(
        start_pos, start_pos + T,
        device=x.device,
        dtype=torch.float32
    )

    frequencies = base ** (
        -torch.arange(
            0, D, 2,
            device=x.device,
            dtype=torch.float32
        ) / D
    )

    angles = positions[:, None] * frequencies[None, :]

    cos = angles.cos()[None, None, :, :]
    sin = angles.sin()[None, None, :, :]

    pairs = x.float().reshape(B, H, T, D // 2, 2)

    a, b = pairs[..., 0], pairs[..., 1]

    rotated = torch.stack([
        a * cos - b * sin,
        a * sin + b * cos
    ], dim=-1).flatten(-2)

    return rotated.to(x.dtype)

Notice the new argument: start_pos.

For prefill, it usually starts at zero.

For the next one-token decode step, it starts at the number of previously cached tokens.

Part B — Cached grouped-query attention

Python

class CachedGQA(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim=64, n_heads=8, n_kv_heads=2):
        super().__init__()

        assert dim % n_heads == 0
        assert n_heads % n_kv_heads == 0

        self.n_heads = n_heads
        self.n_kv_heads = n_kv_heads
        self.head_dim = dim // n_heads
        self.repeats = n_heads // n_kv_heads

        self.wq = nn.Linear(dim, dim, bias=False)
        self.wk = nn.Linear(
            dim, n_kv_heads * self.head_dim, bias=False
        )
        self.wv = nn.Linear(
            dim, n_kv_heads * self.head_dim, bias=False
        )
        self.wo = nn.Linear(dim, dim, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x, cache=None):
        B, T, D = x.shape

        past_length = (
            0 if cache is None
            else cache[0].size(2)
        )

        q = self.wq(x).view(
            B, T, self.n_heads, self.head_dim
        ).transpose(1, 2)

        k = self.wk(x).view(
            B, T, self.n_kv_heads, self.head_dim
        ).transpose(1, 2)

        v = self.wv(x).view(
            B, T, self.n_kv_heads, self.head_dim
        ).transpose(1, 2)

        # Rotate using true positions in the full sequence
        q = rope_with_offset(q, past_length)
        k = rope_with_offset(k, past_length)

        # Append new KV tensors to existing cache
        if cache is not None:
            old_k, old_v = cache

            k = torch.cat([old_k, k], dim=2)
            v = torch.cat([old_v, v], dim=2)

        new_cache = (k, v)

        # Educational GQA: repeat KV heads for matching Q heads
        full_k = k.repeat_interleave(self.repeats, dim=1)
        full_v = v.repeat_interleave(self.repeats, dim=1)

        # Absolute positions are important for cached chunks
        query_positions = torch.arange(
            past_length, past_length + T,
            device=x.device
        )

        key_positions = torch.arange(
            past_length + T,
            device=x.device
        )

        # True means the query is allowed to see that key
        causal_mask = (
            key_positions[None, :]
            <= query_positions[:, None]
        )

        out = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(
            q, full_k, full_v,
            attn_mask=causal_mask,
            is_causal=False,
            dropout_p=0.0
        )

        out = out.transpose(1, 2).contiguous()
        out = out.view(B, T, D)

        return self.wo(out), new_cache

Pay attention to one subtle implementation detail.

When the query contains only one new token but the keys contain 1,000 cached tokens, the attention matrix isn't square.

Using an ordinary lower-triangular mask as though positions started from zero would be incorrect.

Our explicit mask compares absolute query and key positions. PyTorch's attention documentation describes this non-square causal-alignment issue and specifies that True entries in a boolean attn_mask indicate allowed attention. [7]

Our educational implementation explicitly repeats KV heads and concatenates cache tensors. It demonstrates the correct computation but is not an optimal production implementation. Production serving engines manage KV memory using much more efficient allocation and attention kernels.

Part C — Attach it to a complete decoder

We'll keep the RMSNorm and SwiGLU ideas from Lecture 1.

Python

class SwiGLU(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim, hidden_dim):
        super().__init__()

        self.gate = nn.Linear(dim, hidden_dim, bias=False)
        self.up = nn.Linear(dim, hidden_dim, bias=False)
        self.down = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, dim, bias=False)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.down(
            F.silu(self.gate(x)) * self.up(x)
        )


class CachedBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim=64, ff_dim=128):
        super().__init__()

        self.norm1 = nn.RMSNorm(dim)
        self.attn = CachedGQA(dim, 8, 2)

        self.norm2 = nn.RMSNorm(dim)
        self.ffn = SwiGLU(dim, ff_dim)

    def forward(self, x, cache=None):
        attn_out, new_cache = self.attn(
            self.norm1(x), cache
        )

        x = x + attn_out
        x = x + self.ffn(self.norm2(x))

        return x, new_cache


class TinyCachedGPT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size=128, dim=64, layers=2):
        super().__init__()

        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, dim)

        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList([
            CachedBlock(dim=dim)
            for _ in range(layers)
        ])

        self.norm = nn.RMSNorm(dim)
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(
            dim, vocab_size, bias=False
        )

    def forward(self, token_ids, caches=None):
        x = self.embedding(token_ids)

        new_caches = []

        for i, block in enumerate(self.blocks):
            old_cache = (
                None if caches is None else caches[i]
            )

            x, new_cache = block(x, old_cache)
            new_caches.append(new_cache)

        logits = self.lm_head(self.norm(x))

        return logits, new_caches

The new model returns two things:

(logits,new caches)(\text{logits},\text{new caches})

The logits are the same kind of next-token scores as before.

The caches preserve information that future generation steps can reuse.

Part D — Verify cached and uncached computation

This is the most important test.

We don't want to merely show that the cached model runs.

We want to check that it agrees with a full-sequence causal forward pass.

Python

torch.manual_seed(42)

model = TinyCachedGPT().eval()

tokens = torch.randint(
    0, 128, (1, 12)
)

with torch.inference_mode():

    # Compute the entire sequence in one pass
    full_logits, _ = model(tokens)

    # Process the same sequence one token at a time
    caches = None
    pieces = []

    for i in range(tokens.size(1)):
        step_logits, caches = model(
            tokens[:, i:i+1],
            caches=caches
        )

        pieces.append(step_logits)

    cached_logits = torch.cat(pieces, dim=1)

    # Compare all positions
    torch.testing.assert_close(
        full_logits,
        cached_logits,
        rtol=1e-4,
        atol=1e-5
    )

print("Cached and full-sequence logits agree.")
print("Logit shape:", cached_logits.shape)

# Shape: (1, 12, 128)
print("Layer-0 key cache shape:", caches[0][0].shape)
# (1, 2, 12, 8)

This checks that the mathematical results are approximately equivalent, subject to floating-point differences.

It doesn't benchmark speed.

Our small educational model may even run more slowly with one-token cached calls because Python and kernel-launch overheads dominate.

The real benefit becomes important when the model and context are large enough that avoiding repeated computation matters.

Part E — Generate text using the cache

Python

@torch.inference_mode()
def generate_greedy(model, prompt, max_new_tokens=20):
    assert max_new_tokens >= 1
    model.eval()

    # Prefill: process the entire prompt
    logits, caches = model(prompt)

    next_id = logits[:, -1, :].argmax(
        dim=-1, keepdim=True
    )

    generated = torch.cat([prompt, next_id], dim=1)

    # Decode: one newly generated token at a time
    for _ in range(max_new_tokens - 1):
        logits, caches = model(
            next_id,
            caches=caches
        )

        next_id = logits[:, -1, :].argmax(
            dim=-1, keepdim=True
        )

        generated = torch.cat(
            [generated, next_id], dim=1
        )

    return generated


prompt = torch.randint(0, 128, (1, 6))

output = generate_greedy(
    model, prompt, max_new_tokens=10
)

print(output)
print("Output shape:", output.shape)
# (1, 16)

Our random model will produce meaningless token IDs because we haven't trained it.

But the inference mechanism is correct in structure:

Prefill once → Store K/V → Generate one token → Extend K/V → Repeat.

A production generator would additionally handle end-of-sequence tokens, stop strings, context limits, variable-length requests, cache reuse and efficient allocation.

11. Sampling — How do logits become the next token?

We've used greedy decoding:

Python
next_id = logits.argmax(dim=-1)

This always chooses the highest-scoring token.

But modern language models often sample from a probability distribution instead.

Softmax and temperature

For vocabulary logit ziz_i:

Pi=exp⁡(zi/τ)∑jexp⁡(zj/τ)\boxed{ P_i= \frac{\exp(z_i/\tau)} {\sum_j\exp(z_j/\tau)} }

Where τ\tau is temperature.

  • Lower positive temperature makes the distribution more concentrated.

  • Higher temperature makes it flatter.

  • Greedy decoding is treated separately as the deterministic highest-logit choice.

Let's see this.

Top-k sampling

Keep only the kk highest-scoring candidate tokens.

Set the others' probabilities to zero and renormalize.

For k=2k=2, only the two highest-ranked candidates remain eligible.

Top-p sampling

Instead of keeping a fixed number of candidates, sort tokens by probability and retain the smallest leading set whose cumulative probability reaches or exceeds pp, then renormalize.

This is also called nucleus sampling.

If one token already has probability 0.95, top-p = 0.9 might leave only that token.

If the distribution is flatter, many more candidates may remain eligible.

Greedy versus sampling versus beam search

Method

General behavior

Common trade-off

Greedy

Choose highest-probability next token

Deterministic but locally myopic

Temperature sampling

Sample from adjusted probabilities

Controls diversity

Top-k

Restrict to a fixed number of candidates

Excludes the tail

Top-p

Restrict by cumulative probability mass

Adaptive candidate-set size

Beam search

Track several high-scoring sequence hypotheses

More computation, useful in some structured generation settings

One important conceptual point:

A model's next-token probabilities are learned during training; decoding methods determine how we use those probabilities to produce an output.

Changing temperature may make generation more varied, but it doesn't teach the model new facts.

And deterministic decoding doesn't guarantee factual correctness.

12. Three real-world inference troubleshooting scenarios

Now let's apply what we've learned to the kinds of problems that appear in research engineering and technical interviews.

Scenario A — Can an 8B 4-bit model run on an 8 GiB GPU?

Assume:

  • Eight billion parameters.

  • Ideal 4-bit weight storage.

  • 32 layers, eight KV heads, head dimension 128.

  • 8,192-token context.

  • BF16 KV cache.

Our basic calculation gives:

Component

Idealized memory

Weights

3.73 GiB

KV cache, one 8K sequence

1.00 GiB

Subtotal

4.73 GiB

There is space remaining in theory.

But the actual requirement is higher because of weight-quantization metadata, runtime allocations and temporary buffers.

Conclusion: It may fit for one sequence with an appropriate backend, but the simple calculation alone cannot guarantee it.

Now imagine four concurrent 8K sequences.

KV memory becomes 4 GiB:

3.73+4=7.73 GiB3.73+4=\boxed{7.73\text{ GiB}}

That's already almost the full 8 GiB capacity, before overhead.

Four concurrent long-context requests would therefore be unrealistic without further optimizations, lower cache memory use, offloading or different workload constraints.

Scenario B — Why does an 8B model get slower at 32K context than at 2K?

Its parameter count hasn't changed.

But the attention work for every newly generated token grows with the amount of context it must attend over.

The KV cache also becomes larger.

The model has more K/V data to read, and each new query must interact with more previous positions.

So the bottleneck may increasingly involve cache memory bandwidth and attention operations.

Increasing the GPU's arithmetic performance alone may not solve the problem if memory bandwidth is limiting.

Scenario C — Why doesn't quantizing to 4-bit give four times the speed?

Because 4-bit quantization addresses weight storage and potentially weight movement, not every cost of inference.

The GPU still performs attention, normalization, nonlinear activations, sampling and other operations.

It still manages the KV cache.

And quantized kernels may perform dequantization or additional transformations.

Also, the workload may be compute-bound rather than primarily weight-bandwidth-bound.

The practical answer is to benchmark the complete workload, not assume speedup from the number of bits alone.

13. Interview challenge

14. Final mental model

We've now connected the language-model architecture, numerical precision, memory usage and generation process.

1. Prefill processes known prompt tokens.

The GPU can exploit parallel computation across prompt positions and constructs the initial KV cache.

2. Decode generates tokens autoregressively.

Each next-token prediction depends on the previously available sequence.

3. KV caching avoids recomputing previous keys and values.

But each new token still attends to earlier cached positions.

4. KV memory grows with context length, layers and concurrency.

MKV=2BTLHKVdhsM_{\mathrm{KV}}=2BTLH_{\mathrm{KV}}d_hs

5. Quantization reduces parameter storage.

Mweights≈P b8M_{\mathrm{weights}}\approx \frac{P\,b}{8}

Real checkpoints may require additional metadata and use mixed precision.

6. Weight precision and KV precision are separate choices.

A 4-bit model can still have a BF16 KV cache.

7. Quantization doesn't automatically mean faster execution.

Actual performance depends on memory bandwidth, hardware, kernel implementations and workload.

8. Decoding controls output selection, not learned knowledge.

Greedy, temperature, top-k and top-p change how we choose from the next-token distribution.

The discovery that leads to Lecture 4

We now understand how a single model handles inference and how to estimate the memory required for a given context length.

But suppose we're running a public API.

There are 1,000 incoming requests:

  • Some have 100-token prompts.

  • Some have 20,000-token prompts.

  • Some users need 20 output tokens.

  • Others request 2,000.

  • Some requests arrive while others are already decoding.

If we serve requests one at a time, expensive GPUs may remain underutilized.

If we naively batch requests together, some users may wait unnecessarily and KV memory can become fragmented or exhausted.

This creates a scheduling problem, not just a neural-network problem.

Incoming user requests

Different prompt and output lengths

Dynamic request scheduler

Choose which prefills and decode steps execute

GPU workers + Efficient KV memory management

Continuous batching · PagedAttention · Cache reuse

Stream tokens to users

Control latency, throughput and cost

That's Lecture 4 — Serving LLMs at Large Scale.

We'll study how engines such as vLLM schedule requests, how PagedAttention manages KV memory, why continuous batching improves utilization, how speculative decoding works, and how to choose between latency and throughput objectives.

We'll also design a production serving architecture and calculate tokens per second, GPU utilization, concurrency, tail latency and cost per million tokens.

Our central question will change from:

"How efficiently can one model generate text?"

to:

"How efficiently can an entire system serve thousands of users simultaneously?"

Chapter 04

Serving LLMs at Large Scale

Continuous Batching · PagedAttention · Scheduling · Prefix Caching · Speculative Decoding · Distributed Serving · Latency · Throughput · Cost

In Lecture 3, we learned how a Transformer generates text efficiently for one request.

We calculated weight memory, implemented KV caching, compared prefill with decoding, and explored quantization.

Now imagine our model is deployed as a public API.

At 10:00:00, three requests arrive:

Request

Input tokens

Output tokens

A — Short question

10040

B — Research-paper summary

12,0001,000

C — Code completion

2,000150

A moment later, another hundred requests arrive.

We cannot simply treat them as one enormous batch and expect the GPU to operate efficiently.

Some requests are still processing their prompts. Others are generating their 20th or 200th output token. Some finish while new users are arriving.

The challenge is no longer just generating tokens efficiently. It's scheduling thousands of independent token-generation processes on shared hardware.

That's the central problem of LLM serving.

Our journey today

1

Why static batching wastes GPU capacity

2

3

A practical serving simulator and architecture

1. Why not just process requests in batches?

Remember mini-batching from Deep Learning Basics.

Instead of processing each training example independently, we collect several into a tensor and run them through the network together.

This makes matrix multiplications more efficient on GPUs.

At inference time, batching also helps, especially because many sequences can share the same model-weight reads.

But there's a complication.

Different users generate different numbers of tokens.

Suppose Requests A and B begin together:

  • A needs three decode steps.

  • B needs six decode steps.

  • C arrives while they're running.

With a static batch, the system might wait for the whole batch to finish before admitting C.

That's inefficient.

Static batching versus continuous batching

Editorial correction. Request C arrives at step 4. The first three cells in C’s row are marked inactive. In static batching, C queues during steps 4–6.

Here's the key insight:

Why should Request C wait for Request B to finish if Request A has already freed capacity?

It shouldn't have to.

That leads to continuous batching, sometimes called iteration-level or in-flight batching.

2. Continuous batching — Scheduling at each generation step

Instead of treating a batch as a fixed group of requests until completion, the serving engine updates the active batch as execution progresses.

At each scheduling iteration, it can:

  • Continue decoding active requests.

  • Remove completed requests.

  • Admit new requests when resources permit.

  • Schedule prompt-prefill tokens.

  • Respect KV-cache and compute limits.

This allows requests with different arrival times and generation lengths to share GPU resources efficiently.

NVIDIA's TensorRT-LLM documentation explicitly describes in-flight batching as a way to combine context processing and generation for better utilization. [1]

What happens during one iteration?

Imagine the active requests are:

One simplified scheduler iteration

Request

State

Scheduled tokens

ADecoding1
BDecoding1
CPrefilling512

Total

514

Notice the asymmetry.

A decoding request may contribute one token's computation in this iteration, while a prefill request can contribute hundreds or thousands of prompt tokens.

In a token-budget-based scheduler, the engine decides how many tokens can be processed at once, subject to available KV blocks and other limits.

Modern vLLM documentation describes a unified scheduler with a token budget covering ongoing and waiting requests, including chunked prefill and speculative decoding. [2]

The scheduler's three major resources

Compute budget

How many token positions or how much work can the GPU process in the current iteration?

KV-memory budget

Can the system allocate or retain the cache blocks needed by active requests?

Scheduling policy

Which requests get priority, and how do we prevent long requests from making short requests wait indefinitely?

This isn't just a performance problem. It's also a fairness problem.

A scheduler that always prioritizes long prefills might delay interactive users.

A scheduler that always prioritizes decoding might starve newly arriving prompts.

The correct policy depends on the workload and desired service-level objectives.

Important distinction

Batch size, concurrency and throughput are different concepts.

  • Batch size describes how much work is executed together.

  • Concurrency describes how many requests are in progress.

  • Throughput measures how much work is completed per unit time.

Increasing concurrency can improve throughput when hardware is underutilized, but eventually the system reaches capacity and queues begin to grow.

We'll calculate that relationship later.

3. The next bottleneck: KV-cache memory allocation

Continuous batching lets many requests run simultaneously.

But remember our previous lecture's KV-cache formula:

MKV=2BTLHKVdhs\boxed{ M_{\mathrm{KV}}=2BTLH_{KV}d_hs }

The cache grows as tokens are added.

And different requests have different context lengths.

Suppose the system receives requests requiring:

  • 37 cached token positions.

  • 71 cached token positions.

  • 102 cached token positions.

We don't know their final lengths in advance because generation may finish early or continue until a limit.

Why naive memory allocation is wasteful

One naive strategy is to reserve the maximum possible KV memory for every request at admission.

Imagine every request is allowed up to 8,192 tokens.

If a user only needs 200 tokens, reserving the full 8,192-token cache wastes substantial capacity.

A different naive strategy is to repeatedly allocate larger contiguous memory regions as the sequence grows.

That creates allocation and fragmentation problems.

This is the motivation behind PagedAttention, introduced with vLLM. Its design was inspired by virtual-memory paging and allows KV blocks to be stored in noncontiguous physical memory. [3]

The key idea: Allocate KV memory in blocks

Instead of reserving one large contiguous cache for an entire sequence, divide its KV cache into fixed-size blocks.

For example, with a block size of 16 tokens, a 37-token sequence needs:

⌈3716⌉=3 blocks\left\lceil\frac{37}{16}\right\rceil=3\text{ blocks}

Those three blocks provide capacity for 48 positions.

Only 11 token slots are unused.

Interactive: KV-block allocation

Notice something important:

Paging doesn't make the KV cache smaller for the same fully populated sequence.

It makes the allocation of cache storage more flexible and reduces waste caused by over-reservation and fragmentation.

That's a different optimization from GQA or FP8 KV caching.

GQA reduces the number of KV values per token.

FP8 reduces bytes per KV value.

Paging improves how memory is allocated and reused.

Logical versus physical blocks

The request sees a logical sequence:

Logical sequence A

Block 0

Block 1

Block 2

Physical GPU block pool

0

C

1

A₁

2

Free

3

B

4

A₀

5

A₂

The three blocks belonging to Request A occupy physical blocks 4, 1 and 5. They don't need contiguous physical addresses.

The attention kernel uses block-mapping metadata to locate the keys and values associated with the logical sequence.

When a request finishes, its unshared blocks can return to a free pool or become eligible for cache reuse.

In the original PagedAttention paper, this design substantially improved memory efficiency and increased serving throughput in the authors' evaluated workloads. [3]

Interview takeaway: PagedAttention is not the same as FlashAttention.

FlashAttention

PagedAttention

Optimizes the computation and memory movement of attention

Optimizes access to paged KV-cache storage

Avoids naively materializing large attention intermediates

Allows noncontiguous KV blocks and flexible allocation

Central to efficient attention kernels

Central to dynamic multi-request KV management

Both can be relevant to efficient serving, but they solve different problems.

4. Prefix caching — Why recompute the same prompt repeatedly?

We've discovered how to store KV blocks efficiently.

Now consider a different situation.

Suppose your application sends the same 4,000-token system instructions and documentation to every request.

Only the final user question changes.

Two requests sharing an identical prefix

Request A

Shared system instructions + document

Question A

Request B

Same prefix

Question B

Reuse the shared prefix's existing KV blocks

During the first request, the server computes K/V representations for the shared prefix.

When the second request arrives, it may be able to reuse those representations instead of recomputing them.

This is prefix caching.

vLLM's automatic prefix caching is designed around identifying reusable KV blocks from their token contents and preceding prefix context. [4]

Three things to understand

First, prefix caching requires compatible exact prefixes. Two prompts being semantically similar isn't sufficient. Token sequence, positions, model configuration and other cache-validity conditions matter.

Second, it primarily saves prefill computation. Once the requests diverge, their different generated continuations still require decoding.

Third, a cache hit isn't guaranteed. Cached blocks may have been evicted or may be unavailable on the worker receiving the request.

This is also why request routing can affect caching effectiveness: sending requests with the same prefix to completely unrelated GPU workers may prevent local cache reuse.

Prefix caching versus ordinary KV caching

Ordinary KV caching

Prefix caching

Reuses earlier K/V within one continuing request

Reuses compatible K/V across different requests or conversation turns

Avoids recomputing the request's history during decode

Avoids repeating some prompt-prefill work

Useful for almost every autoregressive generation

Useful when requests share cached prefixes

Both use stored K/V tensors, but the reuse scenarios are different.

5. Chunked prefill — The problem with giant prompts

Now imagine Request A is already generating a response smoothly.

Then Request B arrives with a 32,000-token prompt.

If the server processes the entire prompt in one large, uninterrupted prefill operation, Request A may experience a noticeable pause before receiving its next token.

This is called prefill–decode interference.

Prefill and decode have different computational characteristics, as we learned in Lecture 3.

The solution: Split large prefills into chunks

Instead of processing all 32,000 prompt tokens at once, the scheduler can split them into smaller portions.

For example, using a simplified 4,096-token chunk budget:

One long prompt, eight scheduled chunks

Chunk 1

4,096

Chunk 2

4,096

Chunk 3

4,096

Chunk 4

4,096

Chunk 5

4,096

Chunk 6

4,096

Chunk 7

4,096

Chunk 8

4,096

Interleave chunks with active decode requests

The example assumes uniform chunks for simplicity. Real chunk sizes depend on token budgets, available memory and scheduling decisions.

This lets the scheduler interleave prompt processing with output-token generation.

But there's a trade-off.

Smaller chunks can give the scheduler more opportunities to serve interactive decode requests.

However, splitting a prefill may increase scheduling overhead or reduce prefill efficiency.

A very large chunk may improve prefill throughput but produce worse inter-token latency for existing requests.

This is why max_num_batched_tokens and chunked-prefill settings are important serving controls. [5]

Interview takeaway: Chunked prefill primarily changes when and how prefill work is scheduled. It doesn't change the language model's fundamental next-token objective.

6. Speculative decoding — Can we generate multiple tokens per step?

We've now improved batching and memory allocation.

But one fundamental bottleneck remains:

Autoregressive decoding usually advances one new token per target-model step.

What if a cheap model could guess several likely tokens, then the expensive model could verify them together?

This is the idea behind speculative decoding.

The intuition

Suppose the prompt is:

"The capital of France is"

A smaller, faster draft model proposes:

Paris → . → It → is

The large target model then evaluates the proposed continuation in parallel using causal attention.

It can accept a matching prefix and reject the continuation at the first invalid position.

Speculative decoding example

Current prefix: "The capital of France is"

Cheap draft model proposes four tokens

Paris

.

It

is

Target model verifies proposed tokens in one batched forward pass

Paris

.

It

is

In this illustrative greedy-verification case, the first two drafted tokens are accepted. The third is rejected, and subsequent draft tokens are discarded.

Why can this be faster?

Remember the prefill-versus-decode distinction.

The large model is often inefficient when processing only one new query token, especially at low batch sizes.

But it can evaluate multiple proposed positions in one forward pass.

If many draft tokens are accepted, we advance several output positions while paying for fewer sequential target-model invocations.

The draft model does add computation, so the gain depends on its speed and accuracy.

Is speculative decoding lossless?

Under an appropriate exact verification algorithm, speculative decoding can preserve the target model's output distribution, up to numerical effects.

For greedy decoding, verification can compare proposals with the target's greedy choices.

For probabilistic sampling, exact speculative sampling uses an acceptance/rejection procedure involving both the target and proposal distributions, plus a corrected distribution after rejection.

It's not generally correct to accept tokens merely because their target probabilities are above an arbitrary threshold.

vLLM documents distribution-preserving verification and also distinguishes it from explicitly lossy alternatives. [6]

How much speedup can we expect?

Let's construct an intuition-only model.

Suppose a draft model proposes four tokens and each subsequent proposed token has an independent probability a=0.8a=0.8 of being accepted, conditional on all earlier draft tokens being accepted.

The expected number of accepted draft tokens is:

E[A]=a+a2+a3+a4E[A]=a+a^2+a^3+a^4
=0.8+0.64+0.512+0.4096=2.3616=0.8+0.64+0.512+0.4096 =\boxed{2.3616}

In a standard scheme that also produces a target token at a rejection or after full acceptance, the expected number of output positions advanced per verification round is approximately:

1+E[A]≈3.36\boxed{1+E[A]\approx3.36}

under these simplifying assumptions.

But this is not a 3.36× guaranteed speedup.

We must also account for:

  • Draft-model generation time.

  • Target verification time.

  • Acceptance behavior on real prompts.

  • Additional cache and memory overhead.

  • Concurrent serving workload.

At high batch sizes, ordinary target decoding may already use the GPU efficiently, reducing the advantage.

When is speculative decoding most useful?

It can be especially attractive when target-model decoding is expensive and a cheap draft mechanism predicts accepted tokens reliably.

Different methods include small draft models, n-gram-based drafting and architectures with built-in multi-token prediction heads.

These are related approaches, but they don't all require a separate small language model.

7. Prefill/decode disaggregation — Should both phases use the same GPUs?

So far, we have assumed one GPU worker performs both prefill and decode.

But recall the two phases:

Prefill: Large parallel computation over the known prompt.

Decode: Small incremental steps, with repeated weight and KV access.

They have different resource profiles.

What if we assigned different GPU workers to each phase?

This is called disaggregated serving.

Request router

Prefill GPU pool

Process prompt · Construct KV tensors

Transfer required KV state

Over a sufficiently fast interconnect

Decode GPU pool

Continue generation · Stream output

This can isolate the two phases, allowing different hardware or parallelism configurations for each.

It's particularly useful when long prefills interfere with latency-sensitive decoding.

But there's a trade-off: the KV cache must be transferred between workers.

NVIDIA's TensorRT-LLM documentation describes precisely this trade-off between independent optimization of prefill/decode and KV-transfer overhead. [7]

A quick transfer calculation

From Lecture 3, our illustrative 8B architecture needs approximately 1 GiB of BF16 KV storage for an 8,192-token prompt.

Suppose the network provides an ideal 100 Gbit/s data rate:

100 Gbit/s=12.5 GB/s100\text{ Gbit/s}=12.5\text{ GB/s}

Then transferring 1 GiB requires at least approximately:

1.074 GB12.5 GB/s≈86 milliseconds\frac{1.074\text{ GB}}{12.5\text{ GB/s}} \approx\boxed{86\text{ milliseconds}}

This is a theoretical transfer-time lower bound.

Real transfers may be slower due to protocol overhead, contention and synchronization. Different model-parallel layouts may also require additional handling.

So disaggregation isn't automatically worthwhile.

If requests have very short prompts, the transfer overhead might outweigh the benefits.

If requests have massive prefills that disrupt decoding, separating the phases can be highly valuable.

The general engineering lesson: An optimization can improve one latency component while introducing another cost elsewhere.

8. Multi-GPU and multi-node serving — How do we scale beyond one worker?

There are two different reasons to use additional GPUs.

Reason A: The model cannot fit on one GPU.

Reason B: The model fits, but one GPU cannot handle enough requests.

The solution isn't necessarily the same.

Case A — Model parallelism

Suppose a 70B model requires more GPU memory than one accelerator provides.

We could distribute its weight matrices across several GPUs using tensor parallelism, or divide its layers using pipeline parallelism.

We introduced these approaches during Lecture 2.

For inference, the same broad ideas apply, but the performance constraints are different.

Tensor parallelism can require frequent communication between devices during every layer's forward computation.

Pipeline parallelism distributes layers but introduces coordination and pipeline scheduling overhead.

Model parallelism — One logical model across GPUs

GPU 1

Model shard 1

GPU 2

Model shard 2

GPU 3

Model shard 3

GPU 4

Model shard 4

Conceptual illustration. Tensor and pipeline parallelism distribute model computation differently.

Case B — Replication

Suppose our 8B quantized model fits on one GPU.

We can run independent model replicas across several GPU workers.

Each worker can serve its own batch of requests.

Replication — Multiple complete inference workers

Load balancer

GPU 1

Full model replica

Own request queue/cache

GPU 2

Full model replica

Own request queue/cache

GPU 3

Full model replica

Own request queue/cache

Replicas can increase aggregate serving capacity and improve fault isolation.

But they duplicate model weights, and each normally manages its own local KV cache.

This introduces a routing decision.

Should we send requests to whichever worker has the fewest active requests?

Or should we consider cache occupancy, queueing delay, available memory and shared prefixes?

A worker with only two extremely long-context requests might have less available KV memory than a worker with ten short requests.

So routing solely by request count can be suboptimal.

What about MoE?

For an MoE model, expert parallelism can distribute experts across GPUs.

But now token representations may need to travel between devices according to routing decisions.

The relevant bottleneck may become inter-GPU communication and expert load imbalance, rather than just parameter storage.

A useful principle:

More GPUs don't automatically reduce latency. They help when the workload can exploit them without communication, scheduling or load-balancing overhead dominating.

9. Throughput, latency and goodput — The metrics that matter

We've studied a lot of optimization techniques.

But without clear performance metrics, we can't tell whether any of them actually improved the service.

Let's define the most important measurements.

Metric

What it measures

Why it matters

TTFT

Time from request start to first output token

Responsiveness

ITL

Time between streamed token events

Smoothness of generation

TPOT

Average time per output token after the first

Generation speed

E2E latency

Total request-response duration

Overall user waiting time

Request throughput

Completed requests per second

Serving capacity

Output throughput

Generated tokens per second, system-wide

Decode capacity

Queue time

Time waiting for admission/execution

Congestion

KV-cache occupancy

Fraction of available cache memory occupied

Memory pressure

Goodput

Work satisfying defined latency SLOs

Useful service capacity

vLLM exposes many of these through production monitoring metrics, including request counts, queue times, token counts, TTFT, inter-token latency and KV-cache utilization. [8]

Throughput isn't the same as per-user speed

Suppose one GPU produces 40 output tokens per second for one request.

Now we batch eight requests and generate 160 output tokens per second in total.

That's a fourfold increase in total output throughput.

But each user might now receive only around 20 tokens per second on average.

Illustrative throughput trade-off

Scenario

Total output tok/s

Per-user tok/s

1 active request4040
8 active requests16020
Hypothetical values. Actual batching performance depends on the model and hardware.

The GPU is doing more useful work overall, but each individual user may see slower token delivery.

That's the distinction between throughput optimization and latency optimization.

Production systems often need a balance.

Why tail latency matters

Suppose the average TTFT is 300 ms.

That sounds good.

But what if most users receive their first token in 100 ms while a minority wait several seconds?

The mean can hide poor experiences for slower requests.

We therefore often report percentiles such as:

  • p50: Median latency.

  • p95: A latency at or below which approximately 95% of observations fall.

  • p99: A latency at or below which approximately 99% of observations fall.

For an interactive service, p95 or p99 TTFT and inter-token latency may be more important than average latency.

Goodput

Suppose an API has these service-level objectives:

  • TTFT under 1 second.

  • TPOT under 100 milliseconds.

It completes 20 requests per second, but only 12 per second satisfy both requirements.

Then:

Goodput=12 compliant requests/second\boxed{\text{Goodput}=12\text{ compliant requests/second}}

The raw throughput is 20 requests/s, but goodput is only 12 requests/s.

This is why maximizing tokens per second without respecting latency can produce a service that benchmarks well but feels slow to users.

vLLM's serving benchmark supports goodput calculations based on latency objectives such as TTFT, TPOT and end-to-end latency. [9]

10. Queueing theory — Why latency explodes near saturation

Let's connect serving to a fundamental systems concept.

Imagine requests arrive at an average rate:

λ=5 requests/second\lambda=5\text{ requests/second}

Suppose each request spends an average of four seconds inside the system, including waiting and execution.

A famous relationship called Little's Law states:

L=λW\boxed{L=\lambda W}

Where:

  • LL: Average number of requests in the system.

  • λ\lambda: Average effective arrival/completion rate in steady state.

  • WW: Average time spent in the system.

Therefore:

L=5×4=20 concurrent requests on averageL=5\times4=\boxed{20\text{ concurrent requests on average}}

This includes both waiting and running requests.

This is a useful bridge between latency, throughput and concurrency.

What happens when requests arrive too quickly?

Suppose one GPU worker can sustain 10 requests per second under a given workload.

If 5 requests per second arrive, it may operate comfortably.

If 9.5 requests per second arrive, the system is close to capacity.

If 12 requests per second arrive continuously, the incoming demand exceeds its service capacity and the queue will grow unless traffic is rejected, limited or redirected.

Even before reaching the maximum sustainable throughput, queueing latency can increase sharply.

Why?

Because occasional bursts no longer have much spare capacity to absorb them.

The practical lesson: Don't size your serving system to operate permanently at its theoretical maximum throughput.

It needs headroom for traffic variation, long prompts, memory pressure and latency requirements.

11. Capacity planning — How many GPUs do we actually need?

Let's build a simplified serving-capacity model.

Suppose our workload has:

  • Average output length: 300 tokens.

  • Arrival rate: 5 requests/s.

  • Measured hypothetical single-GPU output capacity: 2,000 output tokens/s.

  • Desired operating limit: 70% of that capacity.

The output-token demand is:

5×300=1,500 output tokens/s5\times300=\boxed{1{,}500\text{ output tokens/s}}

The usable capacity per GPU under our headroom policy is:

2000×0.70=1,400 output tokens/s2000\times0.70=\boxed{1{,}400\text{ output tokens/s}}

Therefore:

NGPUs=⌈15001400⌉=2N_{\mathrm{GPUs}}= \left\lceil\frac{1500}{1400}\right\rceil =\boxed{2}

This is only a first-order sizing calculation. In reality, prompt-prefill load, context lengths, KV capacity and latency SLOs could require more resources.

Interactive GPU capacity and cost estimator

Why this calculation is incomplete

Output token capacity is only one constraint.

Suppose each request also contains an average 8,000-token prompt.

At five requests per second, the system receives:

5×8000=40,000 input tokens/s5\times8000=\boxed{40{,}000\text{ input tokens/s}}

The prefill workload might require more GPU resources than the decode workload.

Likewise, many concurrent 8K contexts can consume large amounts of KV memory, even when the generated-output throughput seems modest.

A realistic capacity plan must satisfy all three constraints:

Prefill compute capacity

Decode throughput and latency

KV-cache and GPU memory capacity

The deployment must satisfy every constraint simultaneously.

This is why capacity planning should use measured workloads and actual service-level objectives, not just a GPU's advertised FLOP/s rating.

12. Build a miniature continuous-batching scheduler in Python

We've studied the theory. Now let's simulate the scheduling mechanism.

We'll deliberately keep the model simple so we can focus on the scheduling decision.

Assumptions:

  • Each running request performs one decode step per iteration.

  • At most two requests run simultaneously.

  • Requests have different arrival times and remaining output lengths.

  • We ignore prefill, KV allocation and actual GPU execution time.

We'll compare static and continuous batching.

Python

from collections import deque

requests = [
    {"id": "A", "arrival": 1, "tokens": 3},
    {"id": "B", "arrival": 1, "tokens": 6},
    {"id": "C", "arrival": 4, "tokens": 3},
    {"id": "D", "arrival": 5, "tokens": 2},
]

def simulate(continuous=True, max_running=2):
    waiting = deque()
    running = []
    next_request = 0

    print(
        "\nCONTINUOUS BATCHING"
        if continuous else "\nSTATIC BATCHING"
    )

    for step in range(1, 13):

        # Admit newly arrived requests into waiting queue
        while (
            next_request < len(requests)
            and requests[next_request]["arrival"] <= step
        ):
            request = requests[next_request].copy()
            request["remaining"] = request["tokens"]

            waiting.append(request)
            next_request += 1

        # Release finished requests
        if continuous:
            running = [
                r for r in running
                if r["remaining"] > 0
            ]
        elif running and all(
            r["remaining"] == 0 for r in running
        ):
            # Static: release only when whole batch completes
            running = []

        free = max_running - len(running) if continuous or not running else 0
        for _ in range(min(free, len(waiting))):
            running.append(waiting.popleft())

        executed = []

        # One decode step for each active request
        for request in running:
            if request["remaining"] > 0:
                request["remaining"] -= 1
                executed.append(request["id"])

        print(
            f"Step {step:2d} | "
            f"Decoding: {executed} | "
            f"Waiting: {[r['id'] for r in waiting]}"
        )

        if (
            next_request == len(requests)
            and not waiting
            and all(r["remaining"] == 0 for r in running)
        ):
            break


simulate(continuous=False)
simulate(continuous=True)

Run both configurations.

In continuous batching, completed requests release their capacity immediately at the following scheduling iteration.

In static batching, a finished request can leave an unused position until the rest of its original batch completes.

This simulation isn't an actual GPU serving implementation, but it isolates the scheduling principle.

What would a real scheduler add?

A production scheduler also tracks token budgets, cache-block availability, request priorities, prefill progress, model constraints, cancellation, cache eviction and possibly speculative decoding.

The serving engine then converts those scheduling decisions into efficiently packed GPU computations.

That is substantially more complex than a simple queue.

But the underlying idea remains understandable:

Make scheduling decisions frequently enough that finished or stalled requests don't unnecessarily prevent useful work from progressing.

13. What does a production LLM serving system look like?

Let's assemble everything into one architecture.

Clients

Chat applications · Research systems · Coding assistants · API users

API gateway

Authentication · Rate limits · Request validation · Streaming connections

Inference-aware router

Replica selection · Queue length · Cache awareness · Admission control

GPU worker group A

Scheduler · Model · KV blocks

GPU worker group B

Scheduler · Model · KV blocks

Streaming responses

Tokens delivered as generated · Cancellation supported

Monitoring and autoscaling

TTFT · ITL · p95 latency · GPU utilization · KV occupancy · Errors

Request admission and backpressure

Suppose all GPU workers are full and the waiting queue is growing.

The service needs a policy for handling new requests.

It might queue them up to a configured limit, redirect them to another replica, enforce tenant quotas or reject requests that cannot be served within acceptable limits.

Allowing an unbounded queue is dangerous: memory consumption and request latency can grow even if the model itself is working correctly.

This is called backpressure—preventing incoming demand from overwhelming downstream capacity.

Autoscaling

If incoming demand increases for an extended period, the system may start additional GPU workers.

But GPU autoscaling can be slower and more expensive than scaling an ordinary stateless web service.

Model weights must be loaded, memory allocated and the inference runtime initialized.

So a practical deployment may maintain warm capacity rather than waiting for every burst before launching new workers.

Security and isolation

Production serving also needs tenant-aware authorization, input-size limits, tool permissions, secure handling of prompts and responses, and safe cache reuse.

A shared prefix cache, for example, must not become a mechanism for leaking one tenant's confidential content to another.

We'll explore these trust boundaries in depth in Lecture 7, where we cover prompt injection and LLM application security.

Example: A minimal vLLM service

A basic GPU deployment can expose an OpenAI-compatible API using a command resembling:

Bash

# Requires vLLM, a compatible GPU environment,
# and access to an appropriate model checkpoint.

vllm serve YOUR_MODEL_ID \
  --max-model-len 8192 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 \
  --enable-prefix-caching

The model identifier, memory limits and flags need to match the installed vLLM version and checkpoint requirements.

This runs an inference server, not an entire production platform. Authentication, routing, monitoring, admission policies and deployment management still need to be addressed at the appropriate layers.

For benchmarking, vLLM provides a serving benchmark interface that can evaluate request rates, latency and goodput under different workload settings. [9]

What should we monitor?

In addition to ordinary application logs and error rates, useful engine-level signals include:

Examples of vLLM monitoring metrics

Example

vllm:num_requests_running
vllm:num_requests_waiting
vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc
vllm:time_to_first_token_seconds
vllm:inter_token_latency_seconds
vllm:e2e_request_latency_seconds
vllm:request_queue_time_seconds
vllm:request_num_preemptions
Names reflect current documented vLLM production metrics; availability can differ by engine version and configuration. [8]

These help diagnose why a service is slowing down.

For example:

Symptom

What to investigate

TTFT increases as traffic rises

Queueing, long prefills, admission pressure

ITL spikes during large prompt requests

Prefill–decode interference

KV usage approaches capacity

Long contexts, high concurrency, cache pressure

High preemption counts

KV budget exhaustion or scheduling pressure

Low GPU utilization

Insufficient work, data transfer, scheduling or kernel inefficiency

High throughput but poor user experience

Tail latency and per-request token delivery

One replica overloaded while others are idle

Routing and load balancing

These are diagnostic starting points, not proofs of a particular root cause.

14. Interview challenge — Diagnose a production outage

15. Final mental model

1. Continuous batching keeps GPU capacity productive.

Requests enter and leave dynamically instead of waiting for an entire static batch.

2. PagedAttention makes KV allocation flexible.

Noncontiguous KV blocks reduce over-reservation and fragmentation, improving usable concurrency.

3. Prefix caching avoids repeated prefill.

Compatible requests can reuse KV representations for identical shared prefixes.

4. Chunked prefill reduces interference.

Large prompt computations can be divided and interleaved with latency-sensitive decode requests.

5. Speculative decoding reduces sequential target-model steps.

A cheaper draft mechanism proposes tokens that the target model verifies.

6. Disaggregated serving separates prefill and decode resources.

This can improve phase-specific performance but adds KV-transfer complexity.

7. Throughput, latency and goodput are different objectives.

A server with higher aggregate token throughput can still deliver a worse individual user experience.

8. Production serving is a systems problem.

Efficient models still need scheduling, routing, memory management, admission control, monitoring and capacity planning.

The discovery that leads to Lecture 5

We've built the architecture, learned how to pretrain it, calculated inference memory, and designed a serving system capable of handling many users.

But there's a problem.

Imagine loading a pretrained base language model and asking:

"Explain overfitting to a beginner in three clear bullet points."

The model has learned from massive amounts of text. It may understand overfitting, but it hasn't necessarily been trained to respond reliably to instructions, follow conversational roles or adopt a useful assistant format.

Pretraining teaches token prediction across a broad text distribution.

We now want to teach a more specific behavior:

Given a user instruction, produce an appropriate assistant response.

Pretrained base model

Strong next-token modeling, not necessarily instruction-following

Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)

Instructions · Assistant responses · Chat templates · Loss masking

Efficient adaptation

Full fine-tuning · LoRA · QLoRA

Instruction-following model

That's Lecture 5 — Post-Training I: Supervised Fine-Tuning, LoRA & QLoRA.

We'll trace exactly how conversational examples become supervised training tokens, why certain positions are excluded from the loss, and how adapter-based updates modify a large pretrained model.

We'll also calculate the parameter counts and GPU-memory requirements for full fine-tuning versus LoRA and QLoRA, then implement a real training pipeline.

Our central question will shift from:

"How can we run a pretrained model efficiently?"

to:

"How can we change a pretrained model's behavior without having to train it again from scratch?"
